title: Testamentary capacity disputes - proving a will was validly made
p1:
A signature on a will does not always end the story.

Sometimes the biggest battle begins after the person who made the will is no longer there to explain their decisions.
p2:
Many people assume that if a person signed a will, it must be valid. But the real question in many disputes is whether the person had the mental ability to understand what they were doing at that time.

A person can be elderly, ill, or receiving medical treatment and still have testamentary capacity. Age or a diagnosis alone does not automatically invalidate a will.
p3:
The focus is usually on whether the person understood that they were making a will, knew what assets they owned, and understood who might reasonably expect to benefit from their estate.

One surprising fact: a court may consider medical records, witness statements, and the circumstances around signing the will — not just the final document itself.

A valid will is about more than a signature; it is about proving a clear and informed decision was made.
conclusion: Should evidence of a person’s decision-making ability matter more than their age or health condition when a will is challenged?
